input:
## Start-up

Before the pressure relief valve is placed in service, it is important to ensure that a number of checks have been carried out. In the first place, it should be confirmed from the valve tag and from the equipment record that the valve that has been fitted is the correct valve for this duty. The valve body, the inlet and outlet flange faces and the joint bolts should be inspected carefully for any signs of damage, corrosion or potential leakage paths. It should also be confirmed that no blind, blank or plug that may have been fitted for transport or testing purposes remains in either the inlet or the outlet.

The inlet isolation valve should then be opened fully and sealed in the open position, and the outlet isolation valve should be treated in the same way. It should be borne in mind that a relief valve that can be isolated by means of a partly open valve cannot be regarded as being in service. The discharge line should be walked from the valve outlet to its safe discharge point, in order to confirm that the line is unobstructed, that its drains are free, and that no valve in the discharge path is standing closed. It should also be confirmed that the pressure gauge on the protected equipment is in service.

The equipment should be brought up to pressure in accordance with its own start-up procedure. As the pressure rises, the valve inlet and outlet joints should be checked for leakage, and the valve should be listened to for simmer, which is the audible leakage past the seat that indicates that the valve is close to its set pressure or is passing. Once the equipment is at normal operating pressure and the valve is quiet, the valve should be recorded as being in service in the equipment log.

## Normal operation

During normal operation, the valve remains shut, and the operator's role is essentially one of ensuring that it remains able to act should it be required to do so. Both isolation valves should be kept fully open and sealed open at all times while the protected equipment is live. The valve should be included in the routine rounds, and it should be checked for leakage at the body and joints, listened to for simmer or chatter, checked for icing or deposits at the outlet, and its discharge line should be confirmed as being unobstructed with its drains free.

It is important to note that the set pressure should not be adjusted, that no gag, clamp or blank should be fitted in order to stop a passing valve, and that the inlet isolation valve should not be throttled in order to quieten a valve that is simmering. A valve that passes, that simmers persistently, or that shows damage or heavy corrosion should be regarded as defective; it should be reported, it should be recorded in the equipment log, and its removal and bench test should be planned for the next suitable opportunity.

## Alarms

There are two alarms that concern this valve. The first is the high-pressure alarm on the protected equipment, which warns that the pressure is approaching the valve's set pressure. The action in this case is to act on the equipment rather than on the valve: the pressure should be reduced by the normal operating routes, by cutting the heat input, feed or other pressure source as directed by the equipment procedure, and it should be confirmed whether the valve lifts. If the valve lifts and the pressure steadies or falls, the equipment should be held at the reduced state and the shift supervisor should be informed. If the pressure continues to rise even though the valve has lifted, the equipment should be taken to the safe state that is given in its own procedure.

The second alarm is the discharge alarm, which indicates that the valve has lifted and is discharging, or that it has failed to reseat after lifting. The discharge should be confirmed at the valve and on the discharge line indication, the cause of the overpressure should be found and removed by the normal operating routes, and the discharge indication should be watched until the valve reseats and the discharge stops. If the valve does not reseat and the discharge continues, the equipment should be taken out of service, depressurised by the normal routes, and the valve should be removed for bench test in accordance with the shutdown procedure.

## Shutdown

The valve should be taken out of service only together with its equipment. The protected equipment should first be shut down in accordance with its own procedure, and it should be fully depressurised and drained. It should be confirmed that the equipment is at atmospheric pressure and cannot be repressurised from any connected source before any isolation valve is closed. Only at that point should the inlet and outlet isolation valves be closed, and they should be locked and tagged in the closed position. It should be emphasised that a relief valve should never be isolated from equipment that remains live and capable of being pressurised.

The valve should then be removed under permit, with the joints broken in the order that the permit specifies, and it should be sent for bench test and overhaul by qualified personnel. The open flanges should be capped or blanked while the valve is away. When the valve is returned, it should be refitted with new joint gaskets, and the start-up checks should be repeated in full before the equipment is brought back to pressure.
target:
## Start-up

Place the valve in service only after the protected equipment has been prepared for it. Confirm from the valve tag and the equipment record that the valve fitted is the valve specified for this duty. Inspect the valve body, the inlet and outlet flange faces and the joint bolts for damage, corrosion and leakage paths. Confirm that no blind, blank or plug fitted for transport or testing remains in the inlet or the outlet.

Open the inlet isolation valve fully and seal it open. Open the outlet isolation valve fully and seal it open. A relief valve that can be isolated by a partly open valve is not in service, whatever the state of the rest of the line. Walk the discharge line from the valve outlet to its safe discharge point and confirm that the line is unobstructed, that its drains are free, and that no valve in the discharge path stands closed. Confirm that the pressure gauge on the protected equipment is in service and reading in its normal range for a shut-down vessel.

Bring the equipment up to pressure by its own start-up procedure, not by this chapter. As pressure rises, check the valve inlet and outlet joints for leakage with the equipment's leak-test method, and listen at the valve for simmer, the audible leakage past the seat that indicates the valve is close to its set pressure or is passing. Record the valve as in service in the equipment log once the equipment is at normal operating pressure and the valve is quiet and dry at its joints.

## Normal operation

In normal operation the valve stays shut and does nothing, and the operator's task is to keep it able to act. That task is mostly inspection and restraint: the valve has no routine operation to perform, no stroke to exercise and no setting to trim, and its readiness is preserved by being left alone under watch rather than by being worked. Keep both isolation valves fully open and sealed open at all times while the protected equipment is live. Include the valve in the routine rounds: look for leakage at the body and joints, listen for simmer or chatter, check for icing or deposits at the outlet where the service can produce them, and confirm that the discharge line remains unobstructed and its drains free.

Record the rounds findings in the equipment log, including the nil returns: a log that shows the valve checked and quiet on each round is the evidence that the watch was kept, and a gap in the record is treated at audit as a gap in the watch. Report also any change in the discharge line: a line that runs warm, frosts, or shows fresh deposits at a joint has carried a discharge, whether or not the lift was seen, and the cause is to be looked for as for a witnessed lift.

The valve is bench-tested at the interval the equipment's inspection plan sets, and after any lift that the log records as prolonged or any lift whose cause is not found. Testing is a shutdown activity under the procedure below; there is no in-service test in this chapter, and no device is to be fitted to the valve in service to simulate one.

Do not adjust the set pressure. Do not fit a gag, clamp or blank to stop a passing valve. Do not throttle the inlet isolation valve to quieten a valve that is simmering. A valve that passes, simmers persistently, or shows damage or heavy corrosion is defective: report it, record it in the equipment log, and plan its removal and bench test at the next opportunity the equipment state allows. The valve protects the equipment only in the condition in which it was tested and set, and every unauthorised adjustment removes that protection without announcing the fact.

## Alarms

Two alarms concern this valve, and each has its own action.

The high-pressure alarm on the protected equipment warns that pressure is approaching the valve's set pressure. Act on the equipment, not on the valve: reduce the pressure by the normal operating routes, cutting the heat input, feed or other pressure source as the equipment procedure directs, and confirm whether the valve lifts. If the valve lifts and the pressure steadies or falls, the valve has done its work; hold the equipment at the reduced state and inform the shift supervisor. If the pressure continues to rise with the valve lifted, take the equipment to the safe state given in its own procedure.

The discharge alarm indicates that the valve has lifted and is discharging, or has failed to reseat after lifting. Confirm the discharge at the valve and on the discharge line indication. Find and remove the cause of the overpressure by the normal operating routes, and watch the discharge indication until the valve reseats and the discharge stops. If the valve does not reseat and discharge continues, the equipment cannot be held in service on a passing relief valve: take the equipment out of service, depressurise it by the normal routes, and remove the valve for bench test under the shutdown procedure below.

## Shutdown

Take the valve out of service only with its equipment. Shut the protected equipment down by its own procedure first, and depressurise and drain it fully. Confirm the equipment is at atmospheric pressure and cannot be repressurised from any connected source before any isolation valve is closed. Only then close the inlet and outlet isolation valves, and lock and tag them in the closed position. A relief valve is never isolated from equipment that remains live and capable of being pressurised: the isolation exists for the valve's removal, not for its silencing.

Remove the valve under permit, with the joints broken in the order the permit specifies, and send the valve for bench test and overhaul by qualified personnel. Protect the flange faces and the valve's inlet and outlet during lifting and transport: damage to a seating face in transit returns to service as a valve that passes, and the cause is rarely traced to the journey. Cap or blank the open flanges while the valve is away, and record the equipment as unprotected in the log for the whole of the valve's absence; work that could pressurise the equipment is barred for that period, and the bar is lifted only when the valve is refitted and the start-up checks are complete. On the valve's return, refit it with new joint gaskets, and repeat the start-up checks in full before the equipment is brought back to pressure: correct valve confirmed, blanks removed, isolation valves fully open and sealed open, discharge path clear, and joints leak-tested as pressure rises.
